analysis.one_liner: Lets shareholders sue executives of giant companies over 'woke' political actions, with triple damages and no indemnity.
analysis.headline: The bill drew zero cosponsors, never left the Senate Banking Committee, and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would force the largest public companies (public float over $20 billion or annual revenue over $5 billion) to write new rules into their charters or bylaws as a condition of being listed on a stock exchange. Those rules would make it much easier for a shareholder to sue directors and officers who take political or social stands, such as pulling business out of a state over its election or abortion laws, refusing service to the firearms industry, or promoting diversity programs. In such a suit, the executives would carry the burden of proving they used independent business judgment, could owe at least triple damages or twice the board's total annual compensation, and could not be reimbursed by the company. The bill singles out which corporate actions count: boycotts of China, Russia, and similar countries, defense-related activity, religious exercise, and boycotts targeting Israel are exempt, while actions tied to state election, abortion, or religious-freedom laws and to diversity, equity, and inclusion programs are covered.
analysis.who_benefits: Shareholders who own as little as $2,000 to $25,000 of stock in a large company for one to three years could sue over corporate political conduct, with the company barred from covering the executives' losses, so the penalty lands on the executives personally. Industries that have been targets of corporate boycotts, such as firearms manufacturers and private prison and detention contractors, also benefit, because a large company that cuts them off over a social dispute would face a lawsuit with steep, hard-to-rebut presumptions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Small shareholder activists and boycott-target industries

how_it_helps.text: A shareholder holding $2,000 of stock for 3 years, $15,000 for 2 years, or $25,000 for 1 year qualifies to sue directors and officers for breach of fiduciary duty over covered political actions.

In a covered claim, the corporate defendant must prove it exercised independent business judgment, is bound by statutory presumptions, and, if the shareholder wins, owes at least the greater of treble damages or twice the total compensation paid to all directors that year, plus the shareholder's attorney fees.
Executives cannot be indemnified by the company for any liability from a covered claim, so the financial consequences fall on them personally.

analysis.who_pays: Directors and officers of the largest publicly traded companies bear the new personal liability, and the companies bear compliance costs and litigation exposure. Companies also lose flexibility to make business decisions, such as curbing sales to a state or an industry, when management judges the decision good for the business but the statute presumes otherwise.
analysis.who_pays_short: Executives and boards of giant public companies

drawbacks.text: The bill presumes that workforce morale and retention, board and workforce diversity, public image, and certain investor-driven financial benefits do not count as a company's financial interest, overriding by statute what boards and courts normally treat as legitimate business considerations even when they affect the company's value.

The exemptions are political: identical conduct is treated differently depending on the cause. Limiting business with China, Russia, Iran, and other named countries, defense-related activity, religious exercise, and boycotts targeting Israel are excluded from suit, while actions responding to state election, abortion, or religious-freedom laws and DEI programs are covered.

Treble damages, mandatory fee-shifting, and no indemnification create a litigation weapon that could be used opportunistically or chill ordinary business decisions, since the burden of proving independent business judgment sits with the executives and the statutory presumptions run against them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers a real accountability tool for shareholders who think executives spent the company's money or restricted its business for political reasons, and it targets a genuine gap: fiduciary duties are enforced under state law and usually leave shareholders little leverage over such conduct. But the design undercuts that case. It hard-codes presumptions that diversity, employee morale, and image never serve a company's financial interest, regardless of the facts in a given case, and it exempts conduct favored by one political side while covering conduct disfavored by it. That makes it a culture-war instrument as much as a governance reform, and it would concentrate personal liability on directors and officers of the biggest companies while doing nothing about smaller ones.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced, never got a single cosponsor, and sat without a hearing, markup, or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Marco Rubio introduced the bill on January 31, 2023, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
No senator from either party cosponsored the bill.
The bill received no further action in the committee and never reached the Senate floor; it died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Directors and officers of large public companies avoided a new personal-liability regime, and ESG-focused asset managers, index providers, and union pension funds kept their existing ability to press social and environmental concerns with companies. Industries that had faced corporate boycotts also kept the status quo rather than gaining the lawsuit-backed protection the bill would have given them.

for.name: Sen. Marco Rubio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only supporter in the Senate; no senator cosponsored it.

against.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; it never received a hearing or markup.

against.name: Sherrod Brown
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration during the 118th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had one Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party and never reached a vote, so its partisan support was never tested.

industries.industry: Directors and officers of the largest public companies (public float over $20B or revenue over $5B)
industries.note: The bill would have made them personally liable, with the company barred from indemnifying them, for covered political actions, carrying the burden of proof and facing treble damages or twice the board's total annual pay. Accountability advocates would call that deterrence; the selectivity of what counts as a 'covered claim' made it political exposure.

industries.industry: Firearms manufacturers and other boycott targets (e.g., detention and border-security contractors)
industries.note: A large company that refuses service to these industries over social disputes would face a suit with heavy statutory presumptions and treble damages, making corporate boycotts of them far costlier. Whether that helps the public depends on whether one views such boycotts as activism or as legitimate business responses to public pressure.

industries.industry: ESG asset managers, index providers, and proxy campaigners
industries.note: The bill defines firms whose investment or activism is 'facially unrelated to the pecuniary interest' of the company as nonpecuniary investment entities, presumes related directors are not independent, and presumes financial benefits flowing from such investors do not count. That would sharply limit their ability to press social and environmental goals with big companies.

industries.industry: Labor unions and union pension funds
industries.note: They are expressly listed as nonpecuniary investment entities, and a director affiliated with one is presumed non-independent when deciding whether a shareholder must first ask the board to act. Their shareholder campaigns would have been structurally disadvantaged.
